\framekicker{Learning outcomes}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Session Objectives}
\leadpar{By the end of this session, participants can:}
\begin{isteps}
\item Explain \textbf{progressive disclosure of complexity}, and place yourself on the spectrum of Keras workflows.
\item Build multi-input, multi-output models with the \textbf{Functional API}, and train them with either lists or dictionaries.
\item Use \textbf{access to layer connectivity}: plot a topology with \inlinecode{plot\_model()} and \textbf{extract features} from intermediate nodes.
\item Write a \textbf{Model subclass} --- and name what you give up by choosing it.
\item Write \textbf{custom metrics} (\inlinecode{update\_state}, \inlinecode{result}, \inlinecode{reset\_state}) and \textbf{custom callbacks}, and combine \inlinecode{EarlyStopping} with \inlinecode{ModelCheckpoint}.
\item Write your own \textbf{\inlinecode{train\_step()}} in TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX, and plug it into \inlinecode{fit()} so callbacks and built-in optimisations still apply.
\end{isteps}

\framekicker{Section 7.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{One principle behind the whole API}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/book/figure-7-1.png}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Figure 7.1 --- not four different frameworks, but one spectrum built on shared APIs.~\textcolor{ink3}{\footnotesize---~Chollet \& Watson, \emph{Deep Learning with Python}, 3rd ed. (Manning)}\par}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{You could be using Keras like you would use scikit-learn --- just calling fit() and letting the framework do its thing --- or you could be using it like NumPy, taking full control of every little detail.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 7.1}
\end{iquote}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why that matters for a career, not just a project}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Because every workflow rests on the same \inlinecode{Layer} and \inlinecode{Model} APIs, components from one can be used in any other. \textbf{They all talk to each other.}\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
So what you learn today stays valid once you are an expert. You do \textbf{not} have to switch frameworks going from student to researcher, or from data scientist to deep learning engineer.
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The book's analogy: \textbf{Keras is the Python of deep learning} --- multiparadigm, with several usage patterns that work together rather than one "true" way.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}
\note{Worth repeating: this removes the anxiety of 'will I have to relearn all this later?'}

\coursesection{01}{Three ways to build a model}{Sequential, Functional, subclassing --- and when each is right.}

\framekicker{Section 7.2.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Sequential is essentially a Python list}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}It is the most approachable API, and its limits are equally clear: it can only express models with \textbf{one input and one output}, applying one layer after another.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[amber]
In practice, models with \textbf{multiple inputs} (an image and its metadata), \textbf{multiple outputs} (several things to predict), or a \textbf{non-linear topology} are \hilite{entirely ordinary}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.2.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The Functional API, and the symbolic tensor}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The same two-layer stack, written functionally. The key new object is what \inlinecode{keras.Input} returns.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 7.8 --- a simple Functional model}{listings/ch07-01.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
\inlinecode{inputs} is a \textbf{symbolic tensor}: it holds \hilite{no data at all}, only the specification of the tensors the model will eventually see. Every Keras layer accepts either real tensors or symbolic ones.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.2.2}

\framekicker{Section 7.2.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Layer or Model --- what actually differs}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3196\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3102\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3102\textwidth}}
\thead{} & \thead{\inlinecode{Layer}} & \thead{\inlinecode{Model}} \\ \midrule
Role & A building block used to make models. & The top-level object you train and export. \\
\inlinecode{fit()}, \inlinecode{evaluate()}, \inlinecode{predict()} & Does not have them. & Has them. \\
Saveable to a file & No. & Yes. \\
\end{itable}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Beyond that the two classes are \textbf{virtually identical}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.2.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What subclassing costs you}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{A Functional model} is an explicit data structure --- a graph of layers you can view, inspect, and modify.\par}\vskip 4pt
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{A subclassed model} is \hilite{a piece of bytecode}: a Python class with a \inlinecode{call()} method containing raw code. That is the source of its flexibility, and of its limitations.\par}\vskip 4pt

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{minipage}[t]{1.0\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{Lost when you subclass}
\inlinecode{summary()} \textbf{does not show layer connectivity} $\cdot$ \inlinecode{plot\_model()} \textbf{cannot be used} $\cdot$ \textbf{feature extraction is impossible} --- there is simply no graph.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%

\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[rose]
Once instantiated, the forward pass becomes \textbf{a complete black box}. You are developing a new Python object rather than snapping bricks together, so \hilite{the error surface is much larger}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.3.1 $\cdot$ listing 7.18}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Writing your own metric}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A metric subclasses \inlinecode{keras.metrics.Metric}. Like a layer it holds state in Keras variables --- but that state is \hilite{not updated by backpropagation}, so you write the update logic yourself.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 7.18 --- RMSE as a custom metric}{listings/ch07-12.py}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The next slide names what each of those three methods is responsible for.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.3.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The three methods that form the contract}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{update\_state()}
Called once per batch with the targets and predictions. This is where the accumulation happens.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{result()}
Returns the metric's current value from that accumulated state.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{reset\_state()}
Clears the state without rebuilding the object, so the same instance serves every epoch and both training and evaluation.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[signal]
Unlike a layer, none of this state is touched by backpropagation --- \hilite{you own the update logic entirely}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.3.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{\ldots{}and using it is the same as any built-in}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Custom metrics are passed to \inlinecode{compile()} exactly like the built-in ones, and appear in the progress bar.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{using the custom metric}{listings/ch07-13.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch07-14.txt}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Callbacks: from a paper aeroplane to a drone}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{Launching a training run on a large dataset for tens of epochs using model.fit() can be a bit like launching a paper airplane: past the initial impulse, you don't have any control over its trajectory or its landing spot.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 7.3.2}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A callback is an object passed to \inlinecode{fit()} that Keras calls at various points during training. It can see the model's state and \textbf{act}: interrupt training, save the model, load different weights.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What callbacks are used for}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.241\textwidth}
\begin{icard}
\cardh{Checkpointing}
Saving the model state at different points during training.
\end{icard}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.241\textwidth}
\begin{icard}
\cardh{Early stopping}
Halting when validation stops improving --- and keeping the best model found.
\end{icard}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.241\textwidth}
\begin{icard}
\cardh{Dynamic parameters}
Adjusting things like the optimizer's learning rate mid-run.
\end{icard}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.241\textwidth}
\begin{icard}
\cardh{Logging and plotting}
The \inlinecode{fit()} progress bar you already know is \hilite{itself a callback}
\end{icard}
\end{minipage}%
\icode{python}{some of the built-in callbacks}{listings/ch07-15.py}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Two of these do most of the work in practice, and the next slide shows them used together.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\coursesection{03}{Writing your own training loop}{When fit() is not enough --- and how to keep it anyway.}

\framekicker{Section 7.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Where the built-in loop stops}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\inlinecode{fit()} is built for \textbf{supervised learning}: known targets, and a loss computed from those targets and the model's predictions. Not every form of learning fits that shape.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icard}
\cardh{Generative learning}
No explicit targets at all. Introduced in \textbf{chapter 16}.
\end{icard}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icard}
\cardh{Self-supervised}
Targets are taken \textbf{from the inputs themselves}.
\end{icard}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icard}
\cardh{Reinforcement learning}
Driven by occasional \textbf{rewards} --- much like training a dog.
\end{icard}
\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Two details that break custom loops}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{Pass \inlinecode{training=True} on the forward pass.} Layers such as \inlinecode{Dropout} behave differently during training and inference. \inlinecode{dropout(inputs, training=True)} drops activations; \inlinecode{training=False} does nothing. So: \inlinecode{predictions = model(inputs, training=True)}.
\item \textbf{Use \inlinecode{model.trainable\_weights}, not \inlinecode{model.weights}.} Models hold two kinds: \textbf{trainable} weights updated by backpropagation, and \textbf{non-trainable} weights updated by the layers themselves during the forward pass.
\end{isteps}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Among the built-in layers, the only one with non-trainable weights is \textbf{\inlinecode{BatchNormalization}} --- it tracks the mean and standard deviation of the data flowing through it (chapter 9).
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The shape of a training step}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch07-trainstep.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Identical in all three backends. Only step 3 is written differently.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{TensorFlow and PyTorch, side by side}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Both are close to the pseudocode. The difference is who holds the gradients between steps 2 and 3.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{TensorFlow}{listings/ch07-21.py}
\icode{python}{PyTorch}{listings/ch07-22.py}
\begin{iband}[rose]
\inlinecode{model.zero\_grad()} is \textbf{not optional} in PyTorch: \inlinecode{backward()} adds to the existing gradients, so without it the values pile up and \hilite{training will not proceed}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.4.2 $\cdot$ JAX}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{JAX is harder, and the reason is statelessness}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Because the gradient function is obtained by transformation, you must first write a function that \textbf{returns} the loss. It has to be stateless: everything it uses comes in as an argument, and everything it updates comes back out.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{stateless\_call and value\_and\_grad}{listings/ch07-23.py}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\inlinecode{has\_aux=True} is required because \inlinecode{jax.grad} only accepts functions returning a scalar, and this one also returns the updated non-trainable weights.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.4.2 $\cdot$ JAX}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The optimizer has state too}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Most optimizers track auxiliary variables --- momentum, for instance --- which also have to be threaded through by hand.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{stateless\_apply}{listings/ch07-24.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
The same pattern covers metrics: inside a stateless function you cannot call \inlinecode{update\_state()}, so Keras provides \hilite{\inlinecode{stateless\_update\_state()}, \inlinecode{stateless\_result()}, and \inlinecode{stateless\_reset\_state()}}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Using metrics at the low level}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Outside \inlinecode{fit()}, metrics are driven by hand: update per batch, query when you want a number.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}

\begin{iband}[amber]
Remember \inlinecode{metric.reset\_state()} \textbf{at the start of each training epoch and at the start of evaluation}. Forgetting it \hilite{mixes numbers across epochs} and quietly misleads you.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 7.4.4 $\cdot$ listing 7.21}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Override train\_step(), keep fit()}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Subclass \inlinecode{keras.Model}, replace the one method \inlinecode{fit()} calls per batch, and return a dictionary of metric names to values. Everything else keeps working.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 7.21 --- a custom train\_step}{listings/ch07-29.py}
\begin{ibullets}
\item Works whether you build with \textbf{Sequential, Functional, or subclassing}.
\item You do \textbf{not} need \inlinecode{@tf.function} or \inlinecode{@jax.jit} --- \hilite{the framework applies it for you}.
\end{ibullets}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Summary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What has to survive this chapter}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{Progressive disclosure of complexity} --- one spectrum of workflows over the shared \inlinecode{Layer} and \inlinecode{Model} APIs, not several frameworks.
\item \textbf{Sequential} for simple stacks; \textbf{Functional API} for graphs of layers, and that is what the rest of the book uses; \textbf{subclassing} for anything that is not a graph.
\item Functional gives \textbf{access to layer connectivity}: \inlinecode{plot\_model()} and feature extraction. Subclassing \hilite{forfeits both}.
\item The best combination in practice: \textbf{a Functional model containing subclassed layers}.
\item \textbf{Custom metrics} = \inlinecode{update\_state} / \inlinecode{result} / \inlinecode{reset\_state}. \textbf{Callbacks} = the six \inlinecode{on\_*} hooks.
\item \textbf{\inlinecode{EarlyStopping} + \inlinecode{ModelCheckpoint}} replaces the wasteful train-twice pattern.
\item Writing \inlinecode{train\_step()}: remember \textbf{\inlinecode{training=True}} and \textbf{\inlinecode{trainable\_weights}}; in PyTorch \textbf{\inlinecode{zero\_grad()}}; in JAX everything goes through the \textbf{\inlinecode{stateless\_*}} family.
\end{isteps}
